title: A white-hot sun path, white-headed meteors over point stars, the frost gem slider, minimal HUDs and thick boss bars
intro: This round answers your round 15 notes with the critic's work order on the sky, copying from BSL, Complementary and Photon. What is new in how it was made: the critic judged every sky change inside the loop, against BSL and Complementary on the same views, and what it passed became a default, except the dusk shore's last change (see that scene); each scene says in one line what it passed, with the numbers. The sea, the sun and the meteor night passed the critic in the loop. The dusk shore passes the critic's numbers but not its eye (6/10), and work on it continues next round. Costs are per frame, against the same view with shaders off, and they got a little worse. Worst frames: High at 1440p 3.77 ms (budget 3.0, over; round 15 3.65), Low at 1080p 0.99 ms (budget 0.9, over; round 15 0.95), Potato at 720p 0.33 ms (budget 0.4). 14 of the 24 High views are over 3.0: 12 with open water in view (3.01 to 3.77 ms) and the night views (night new 3.09, night wide 3.02) (round 15: 11). Water is still the main cost on High, as in rounds 14 and 15, and making it cheaper is still your open question. Against round 15's pack in the same run, the sunset views with water cost about 0.11 ms more: the sea 3.62 to 3.73, the shore 2.89 to 3.01, the clear sunset 3.39 to 3.50; the white sun path is +0.07 ms of that and the darker dusk sky +0.03 ms. Views without a low sun (golden lit, plains noon, torch) did not change. The worst High view is sun clear at 3.77 ms. Low views over 0.9: lake glitter 0.96 ms, ocean sunset 0.99 ms (round 15: ocean sunset 0.95, lake glitter 0.94).

scenes.name: The sun's path on the sea: white-hot, all the way to the horizon
scenes.question: Round 15's path was still orange. The critic found two causes: our sun never burned to white (its brightest pixels 253,214,162, BSL's 255,254,251) and the sea beside the path was too orange. Now, at golden hour, the hottest pixels burn to white the way film and BSL's tone curve do, the path's hot core is brighter so it clips white and keeps gold only at its edges, the sea near the sun's bearing eases toward warm white, the island's shadow on the water has a soft edge instead of a hard straight diagonal, and the exposure meter ignores the white core so the frame does not darken. Critic, inside the loop: PASSED, 8/10 (frame s16r3): 41 % of the lit band is white (BSL 34 %), the white column reaches the horizon (649 px, BSL 1325), the frame is within 1 % of its old brightness, and the path's ripple streaks vary about as much as BSL's (0.11 to 0.14 across a frame pair, BSL 0.14 to 0.15; the number moves with the waves). C and D: the path at 2x; E: the island's shadow edge at 2x. Cost on High: this view 3.73 ms (the sun-path changes off 3.66, round 15's pack 3.62, same run). A new (default), B round 15.
scenes.notePrompt: Is this the white-hot path you wanted? (The critic notes the sea round it is olive-khaki where BSL's is amber-rose: next round.)

options.critic: Critic 8: The leap you asked for, and the same picture the critic passed inside the loop (s16r3). The sun's path is now a white column that reaches the horizon, broken into ripple streaks, with gold only at its edges: the same kind of path as BSL's. On this frame 39 % of the lit band is white (BSL 34 %), the white reaches the horizon (646 px), and the frame's brightness is unchanged (100.1). The island's shadow on the water no longer has round 15's straight white wedge; at 2x its edge breaks along the ripples. What still separates it from BSL: the sea round the path is olive-khaki (105,81,43 to the right of the path, the same as round 15) where BSL's is warm amber-rose, and the path is a little more solid than BSL's on this frame (ripple variation 0.11 here, 0.13 on its pair, BSL 0.14-0.15). scenes.question: The same settings act on the clear-sky sunset: the glint under the sun is now a white column broken into ripple streaks, as BSL's, where round 15's was a narrow gold thread. It keeps what you picked in round 14 (B, the wavering on the horizon blocks). Critic, inside the loop: PASSED, 8/10 (frame s16r3cc): the sand block's top edge sits at row 29.6 (your pick 28.8), its heat-shimmer measure is noisy from run to run (0.69 to 1.10 on the same settings; your pick 0.83), so judge it on the crops, the frame is not darker (93.4), and the sun's white disk is 3065 px (BSL 2137). The white runs further down the frame than BSL's (6152 px against 4075); the critic judged that by eye as the same kind of column, not a flat bar. A and B: 2x round the sun; C and D: the column under it at 2x; E and F: the sand under the sun at 2x, this round against round 15's D (your round 14 pick). scenes.name: A darker, warmer dusk sky with gold only on the low clouds (not yet passed by the critic's eye)
scenes.question: The critic, after round 15: the open sky had gone pink-lilac (137,100,103 between the clouds, BSL's warm brown 115,85,57) and was about 1.7 times as bright as BSL's at the top right; the trouble was too much red, not too little blue. Now, with the sun under 7 degrees, the open sky behind the clouds is darkened and drained toward a warm mauve-brown, the low clouds keep their gold, and a high cloud lit as if the sun stood high is brought down to the sky's own level and colour, as BSL's high clouds are at sunset. Critic, inside the loop: 7/10 at its loop 2 (frame s16z11b), 5 of 6 targets passed, failing only on one pale salmon cloud at the top right; it set loop 3's targets (top right luma at most 80, red at most blue + 16, no pixel above luma 120). Loop 3 (frame s16y29) meets all six on the critic's own measuring script: top right 72,60,56 (BSL 66,55,58), no pixel above 120 (was 8455), open sky 63,54,53, blue over green in 7.5 % of the upper sky (limit 15), the sky 0.67 of round 15's brightness (BSL 0.75), rims 240,145,64, clouds keep their colour (saturation 0.57, none grey). Two of those pass by a hair: the top right's red is 15.97 over its blue (limit 16) and the open sky's 10.1 (floor 10), so they will move with small changes. The critic's own fix (darken high cloud by elevation, keeping its hue) could not pass: the pale cloud is thin, so most of its light came through the open-sky part, and even at the sky's brightness its colour kept the top right too red; so it now takes the open sky's mauve above 30 degrees, and the top of the sky has a little less red. The big gold cloud on the right keeps its shape and rims; its upper part is about 4 levels darker. Critic, loop 3: the six numbers pass, but by eye it scores 6/10 and does not pass. The unlit high cloud is darker than the sky behind it (60,46,34 against 69,60,58) and reads as a smudge of smoke, where BSL's high clouds are a little lighter than its sky. The big cloud over the tower is storm grey (71,57,49, BSL 118,88,59). So the dusk shore has not passed the critic: it meets the numbers but fails by eye. A fourth and last pass (a floor, so no cloud falls under the sky behind it, lit clouds leaning tan) turned the big cloud on the left tan but left the top right brown, and it broke two numbers (the top right's red 23 over its blue, limit 16; 21 pixels over 120), so it is not the default and not shown. C and D: the top right at 2x. Cost on High: this view 3.01 ms (the change off 2.98, round 15's pack 2.89). A new (default), B round 15.
scenes.notePrompt: Is this the dusk you wanted: darker, warm, gold only low? Does the unlit high cloud at the top right read as a cloud or as a dark patch?

options.critic: Critic 6: It passes every number and fails by eye. The numbers first: on this frame the top right is 69,59,58 (BSL 66,55,58), no pixel is above 120, the open sky is 63,54,53, blue beats green in 7 % of the upper sky (limit 15), the sky is 0.67 of round 15's brightness (BSL 0.75), and the rims are 238,145,66. The lilac dome is gone and the open sky is in BSL's warm mauve-brown family: that part is fixed. But the clouds went with it. The pale high cloud at the top right is now darker than the sky around it (its core 60,46,34 against the open sky's 69,60,58), so it reads as a smudge of smoke, not a cloud. BSL's high clouds are lighter than its sky (its upper sky's median is 91,70,59, ours 64,56,56). The big cloud over the tower is storm grey, 71,57,49 against BSL's golden tan 118,88,59. The whole frame reads as smoke at dusk, not a sunset. My loop-3 fix (darken high cloud by elevation) was the wrong one, and draining the cloud to the sky's mauve made it worse. It needs to be lit tan and a little lighter than the sky behind it, not darker. C, the top right at 2x, is aimed right and shows the smudge plainly. Cost 3.01 ms (the dusk change +0.03).

scenes.name: White-headed meteors with emerald trains, over point stars
scenes.question: The critic, after round 15: the meteors were yellow, not white heads with green trains, the stars were soft 6x4 px diamonds where Complementary's are pinpoints, and the sky was too dark. Now the shower night is navy, each streak is an emerald body and train behind a white-hot head, and the star field is drawn as points about 2 px across. Critic, inside the loop: PASSED, 8/10 (frame s16t1): the sky's median is 17,23,37 (target 18,22,38), every head in frame is white (243 and 229), the trains are emerald, no star is a soft blob, and the shower night cost 2.97 ms in the loop (target: round 15's 2.98). It left two taste calls to you: at 5x the points are hard 2x2 squares, and five emerald streaks in one view is a lot of green. Cost on the wide night view, shower forced, one run: A 2.98 ms (round 15's pack 2.93); in these clips A 2.99 ms, B 2.98 ms (B is round 15's own clip, from its run). C and D: the Milky Way's stars at 2x. A new (default), B round 15, same view, same radiant.

scenes.name: Gems: frost to calmed, close up
scenes.question: You picked frost and asked for a slider from it toward round 14's calmed look. A to F are that slider in six even steps: every step moves colour, the streak pattern, surface relief and gloss together by the same amount, and each is a complete connected look. Same light as round 15 (late afternoon, the sun ahead). The shader now fades its gem lighting in along the same steps (a fifth per step), so there is no jump between any two neighbours. Only brightness steps evenly: colour moves most in the first steps and glitter late. Sparkle grows the way the eye counts it, roughly doubling each step from C on (frost has almost none until C, F the most). A is round 15's E and F round 15's D. Close: a lone diamond (right) and emerald (left) block, a step away. Look for: where along the slider the stone stops reading as frosted ice and starts reading as a gem, and where it starts to get busy. How the numbers are read (the same measures as round 15, so A and F are round 15's E and D): 'colour' is the mean saturation of the gem pixels (0 grey, 1 pure colour); 'brightness' their mean; 'glitter' how much the brightness jumps from texel to texel (noise); 'sparkles' single bright points per 10 000 gem pixels; 'white' the share of gem pixels that are bright and colourless (glare).
scenes.notePrompt: Which step is right? If it lies between two, say which two.

options.label: Frost (0 %, round 15 E)
options.desc: Your pick: Soartex's frosted gems, pale, matte, a soft sheen (smoothness 140, F0 10), flat. The slider's start. Our read: pale ice with soft marbling and Soartex's diagonal facet lines on the lone block; calm and clean, the diamond nearly grey-blue, the emerald a milky jade. Same as round 15's E (the whole frame, grass included, is about 0.02 brighter: the shader's light moved a little since round 15, not the gem). Measured on this frame, diamond: colour 0.39, brightness 0.54, glitter 0.020, 6 sparkles per 10k px, white 1.9 %; emerald: colour 0.42, brightness 0.47, glitter 0.018, 6 sparkles per 10k px, white 0.0 %.
options.noCost: texture comparison, shot mode: not measured
options.critic: Critic 5: Your pick (round 15's E), unchanged except that the whole frame's light is 0.02 brighter. Pale frosted ice with Soartex's diagonal facet lines: calm and clean, but the diamond is nearly grey-blue (colour 0.39) and the emerald a milky jade. Your taste overrides mine here; I rate it as I did in round 15.

options.desc: Frost's veining with a fifth of round 14's streaks showing through, the colour a fifth of the way to D's deep gem colour, a fifth of D's surface relief, a little more gloss (smoothness 170, F0 14); the shader gives it a fifth of the gem lighting. Our read: still frost, a clear step richer in colour and a touch darker; the marbling and facet lines unchanged in feel, no more sparkle than A. Frost with more gem colour. Measured on this frame, diamond: colour 0.50, brightness 0.50, glitter 0.021, 4 sparkles per 10k px, white 0.2 %; emerald: colour 0.54, brightness 0.42, glitter 0.019, 7 sparkles per 10k px, white 0.0 %.

scenes.name: HUD: four minimal designs
scenes.question: Back to minimal, as you asked, but finished: no bands, cells or ornaments behind the rows (round 15's mistake) and no Elden Ring parts (round 14's grace strip and diamond finials are gone). The polish goes into the icons themselves (one light, glossy or cut shading, a clean keyline) and into one quiet hotbar per design. A starts from round 14. The medallion you liked stays, smaller and cleaner. Each frame also shows one of the four new boss bars (rated separately below). Honest note: at play size the heart and food rows of the four read nearly alike (the shading differs only up close, below); the designs part in the hotbar, selection, XP bar, medallion and boss bar. Needs your yes: the XP number's colour, the XP medallion and the whole boss bar (frame, medallion, percent, outlined name) are drawn by a small client-only hook in qf-content (XpBarStyle.java), not by the texture pack. It is code, so it ships only with your yes. Without it the number is plain lime with no medallion, and the boss bar falls back to vanilla's thin 182 x 5 strip (in each design's colours) with a plain white name; the rest of each HUD (icons, hotbar, XP bar) is texture and stays.
scenes.notePrompt: Which HUD (or which parts of which)? Ship the XpBarStyle hook (yes/no)?

scenes.name: Boss bars after Infernum: bright sky (top) and night (bottom)
scenes.question: Four thick boss bars, our own art, each shown over a bright cloud and over a night sky, the name outlined in all four. Studied from Infernum Mode's own source and sprites (github.com/InfernumTeam/InfernumMode, Content/BossBars; study only, nothing copied): what makes its bar work is one THICK bar (not a line), heavy bevelled rails, a dark but coloured empty channel so the bar reads whole at any health, a slanted stepped sheen on the fill, a bright cap riding the fill's edge, a medallion the fill drains toward, and the health in percent instead of a number. It shows no name; ours keep the name, outlined. Infernum's per-boss head icon, phase pips and enrage fire need data 1.7.10 does not have (it knows only a name and a health fraction), so every boss shows the design's emblem and the rails carry quarter ticks. The bar fades in over a second when a boss appears (not visible in a still). Needs your yes: the XP number's colour, the XP medallion and the whole boss bar (frame, medallion, percent, outlined name) are drawn by a small client-only hook in qf-content (XpBarStyle.java), not by the texture pack. It is code, so it ships only with your yes. Without it the number is plain lime with no medallion, and the boss bar falls back to vanilla's thin 182 x 5 strip (in each design's colours) with a plain white name; the rest of each HUD (icons, hotbar, XP bar) is texture and stays.
scenes.notePrompt: Which boss bar (or which parts of which)?

options.noCost: texture comparison, shot mode: not measured
options.critic: Critic 7: A thick molten bar with a bright cap riding the fill's edge, a flame medallion and the percent after the point. It reads whole at any health and has real heat. At 8 % the fill is a sliver beside the medallion, but the empty channel still shows the bar.

options.label: Obsidian
options.desc: Round 15's obsidian (your 'kinda close') grown into a thick bar: black glass rails with a violet edge light, a magenta fill with a slanted sheen, a crystal shard riding its edge, an octagonal amethyst socket with a slit eye, three crystal spikes at the end, the percent inside the bar.
options.noCost: texture comparison, shot mode: not measured
options.critic: Critic 6: Your 'kinda close' obsidian, now thick: black glass rails, a crystal shard on the fill's edge, an amethyst eye. It still fills magenta-pink, not blood red, so it reads as a mana bar more than health.

options.label: Ironclad
options.desc: Riveted gunmetal rails, a blood-red fill cut into tenths, a steel collar riding its edge, a steel heater shield with a chevron, a square end clamp holding the percent.
options.noCost: texture comparison, shot mode: not measured
options.critic: Critic 5: Riveted rails, a fill cut into tenths and a square percent clamp: it reads as an MMO health bar, the furthest of the four from Infernum's single sheened bar.

options.label: Gilded
options.desc: In our reading, closest to what makes Infernum's bar work: bevelled gold rails, a crimson fill with a slanted stepped sheen over a dark wine channel, a gold cap riding its edge, a round gold-ringed medallion with a horned skull that the fill drains toward, a pointed end, the percent in a gold-rimmed tab under the end.
options.noCost: texture comparison, shot mode: not measured
options.critic: Critic 7: Bevelled gold rails, a crimson fill with a slanted sheen over a dark wine channel, a gold cap on its edge, and a horned-skull medallion the fill drains toward. Of the four, it fits the page's list of what makes Infernum's bar work best. I have not opened Infernum's source, so I judge it against that list, not against Infernum itself. The name reads over the white cloud.
